The cultural currents with which Christianity competed - not only in Alexandria - during the 11th centuries and the first half of the 111th, can be grouped into two large blocks. On the one hand, those from an external sphere to Christianity itself - pagan religions and Judaism, philosophical currents - and, on the other, those that must be combated from its own internal sphere, especially Christian Gnosticism and Montanism. During the 11th century, Christian literature was especially characterized by its apologetic character. It was aimed at the outside world, both to stop the aggressive attitude of paganism, to justify before the State and before the majesty of the Emperor the possibility of a new cult, to respond to the criticisms of superstition and fanaticism with which philosophers branded it 6, as well as. especially, to dispel the opinion that Christianity was a growing threat against the universal Empire of Rome. But Christian literature was also evidently directed towards the interior of the church itself, especially in antiheretical works. This double response, external and internal at the same time, forces Christians to lay the foundations of Thus. For example. the work of Lucian of Samosata, On the Death of Peregrinus (aiio 170). For example, Cornelius Fronton of Cirta in his Discourse. or the Platonist Celsus in his book True Doctrine (year 178), where he states: «when adhering to a doctrine it is necessary to let oneself be carried away by reason; If not, one falls into all kinds of dark practices and one allows oneself to be deceived by perverse people" (collected by ORIGINS. in Contra Celso 19).

They built their synagogues, marking distinctions with the Greek people. In Leontópolis, for example, Onías, in 160 BC. Starting in the 1st century, the number of Jews increased considerably, until, after the Christian Era, they managed to occupy more than two of the five neighborhoods of Alexandria. Jewish law continued to prevail within the synagogues, often supplanting that of the Greek courts, until it became an officially agreed upon law. Since the 1st century AD. C., the Jews were not considered simple metics, but due to their large number they formed a polyteuma, thus becoming almost autonomous "settlers." The Jewish polytheumata were governed by an ethnarch or by a small board of archons. However, in Alexandria they never achieved full citizenship, since this included the worship of the city's gods. On the other hand, they did have kopoliteía or potential citizenship, by which their previous apostasy made them full citizens. The Jewish reaction to Hellenism also provoked its own internal apologetic movement, where an attempt was made to demonstrate the superiority of the Bible over philosophical doctrines (Aristobulus, for example, in 150 BC), or to reconcile Platonism and Stoicism with the Jewish faith.

Finally, by matching the teaching of the LogosMaster with the true Gnosis, Clement seems to try to take advantage of the Gnostic doctrine of the time, which affirmed that divine reality (First Principle or Superprinciple) manifests itself in Intelligence (No&) and Word (Lógos) or Primordial Man. 35.contenido: The paidagogds (in Latin, paedagogus) designated in Antiquity (where the aristocratic lifestyle was recognized) the servant, usually a slave. The pedagogue was in charge of "leading the child" to school. It was about helping the young master carry his small suitcase, the flashlight to light the way, or even carrying the child himself. But, above all, its role was to protect him against the dangers of the street, both physical and, especially, moral. Since Greek immorality frequently affected children, the pedagogue's mission was to ensure the behavior of the child.

36.contenido: boy and in demanding correct and dignified manners from him. Ancient custom therefore attributed moral implications to this requirement. Hence, the "pedagogue" easily went from being a mere companion to becoming a trainer of character and morality. This rise in the consideration and importance of its role as a basic element of childhood education took real form, under the era of Hellenism and the Roman Empire, in the figure of the paedagogorum custodia. The pedagogue now complemented the work of parents and teachers. According to Quintilian, the pedagogue is not separated from the child even at home, he can, at times, also perform the role of repeater or studiorurn by giving him homework or studying the lesson, always - of course - subordinated to the directives of the qualified teacher or didáskalos. However, the technical service of an instructor or teacher, financially remunerated, was never properly considered education, nor even well regarded. It was considered a humble and despised job, precisely because it was a job in the commercial sense of the term, because it was paid. Especially in the case of pederasty, but not necessarily only in that case, for the Greek world education resided in “the deep and close relationships that personally united a young spirit with an older person, who was at the same time its model, its guide and its initiator))17. Fundamentally, education consisted of moral training, the formation of character and lifestyle. Therefore, the figure of the pedagogue in Greece responds

41.contenido: Is it not also true that some, such as Justin, Clement, Origen or Hippolytus of Rome, did not give up trying to create a higher school of Christian theology capable of overshadowing the high pagan philosophical culture or the heretical Gnostic movement itself? Thanks to the Oratio panegirica (Farewell Address) of the Cappadocian Gregory the Wonderworker, we know the system of theological teaching that Origen followed in Caesarea. After an exhortation to philosophy, he continued with a preliminary course that trained students for scientific education through constant mental exercise; Finally, the scientific course included logic and dialectics, natural sciences, geometry and astronomy and, finally, ethics and theology. According to J. Quasten, «the ethics course was not reduced to a rational discussion of moral problems, but rather provided an entire philosophy of life))39. Thanks to Eusebius, we know that Origen ingeniously adapted to this school the characteristic methods of higher education of the Hellenistic type. There is, therefore, no doubt that, both in the author of The Pedagogue and in Origenes and others, there was clearly the intention of proposing an alternative pedagogy to that of the time, although this objective was not achieved, for different reasons, until the appearance of the monastic school of the East with the Desert Fathers in Egypt. However, the most ambitious plan of Clementine theology and of Origen himself did not lie in the mere possibility of proposing an alternative high school (in this case, of theology) but - in Jaeger's words - in

51.contenido: 5. Structure of the work The Pedagogo is a work clearly divided into two parts. The first, which corresponds to book 1, is a long preamble that grounds and justifies the role of a Christian pedagogy and its main characteristics. Books 11 and 111 make up the second part and respond to the announced and specific theme of the action of the "Pedagogue", that is, they attempt to be a broad treatise on practical morality, designed especially for the young Christian from Alexandria. Because, in the same way that the pagan life has duties, Christianity, to achieve the "happy" life, must know the Christian duties: "The (duties) that are prescribed for the pagan life are already known by almost everyone; but those relating to the happy life, and thanks to which eternal life is conquered from above, we can examine them schematically, starting from the Scriptures themselves)) (Pet. 1 13, 103).

55.contenido: Both objectives pursue the Pedagogue's own goal: the health or improvement of the soul, which distinguishes it, at the same time, from the task of the Logos-Teacher, because - Clement affirms - "health and knowledge are not the same; The former is obtained by healing (Pedagogue), this, on the other hand, by study (Teacher))". Obtaining this goal allows us to establish, in turn, a double-directed ethical hierarchy - ascending or descending, depending, respectively, on whether we focus our attention on the greater or lesser model - composed of: 1) that of the one who does not commit the slightest fault (God), 2) that of the one who does not commit any deliberate sin (the wise man), 3) that of those who do not commit too many involuntary faults (the well-educated), 4) that of those who remain in sin for the shortest possible time (the recent convert). In the second part, Clement moves on to the description and advice of specific duties, which, without a doubt, allows us today to possess, probably, one of the best frescoes of daily life of the time.

250.contenido: We have seen that the Logos is just, and that his warnings exhort us to salvation, and how, through them, he wants, by the will of his Father, to make us know what is beautiful and useful. Now look at this: what is beautiful is typical of the encomiastical genre, and what is useful is typical of the deliberative genre. The deliberative genre takes two forms: one persuades and the other dissuades; the encomiastic genre can be censorship. Deliberative intelligence is partly hortatory and partly dissuasive. Likewise, the encomiastic genre sometimes takes the form of censure and, sometimes, the form of praise. The righteous Pedagogue, who seeks our good, is especially concerned with all this. As we have already spoken 4 before about the genre of censure and that of dissuasion, we must now consider the hortatory and laudatory genre, thus balancing, as in a scale, the two equal pans of the Just. 756.contenido: HYMN OF CHRIST THE SAVIOR, ACCORDING TO SAINT CLEMENTE Bridle of untamed foals, wing of birds that do not wander, authentic rudder of ships, shepherd of the King's lambs. King of Saints, Omnipotent Logos, Son of the Most High Father, Prince of wisdom, Strength of the weak, eternally accommodating, of human lineage, Savior Jesus, Shepherd, Farmer, Helm, Bridle, Heavenly Wing of the holy flock. Fisherman of mortals, of those who are saved from the sea of ​​evil; To the pure fish in the midst of the adverse waves, cast the hook for a sweet life.

Sacred food of those who praise God in respectful lives. Christ Jesus. Heavenly milk of sweet breasts of the charms of a maiden, squeezed by your Wisdom. Creatures, in tender mouths bred, with the fresh spirit of the spiritual bosom satiated; simple praises, authentic hymns, to Christ the King, holy rewards for his teaching of Life, let us sing in unison. Let us accompany the powerful Child in procession with simplicity, as a Choir of Peace, the children of Christ, a prudent people, and let us all sing together a psalm to the God of peace.
